blogs.title: When Block Diagrams Aren’t Enough: Fed. Cir. Nixes PIM Verdict Over Expert Contradictions
blogs.description: The panel reversed on the ’134 patent because Finesse’s expert tied the claimed “interference generating signals” to a modeled PIM path created downstream of the RF ADC—after sampling—so the receiver could not have sampled those signals as claim 1[a] requires. His mid-cross pivot to generic “x1/x2” inputs never clearly mapped those variables to the claim’s “signals of interest” and “interference generating signals,” and the district court’s inference could not cure self-contradictory testimony. Citing Johns Hopkins v. Datascope, the Federal Circuit underscores that ambiguous, shifting expert mappings—especially those lifted from legends in vendor diagrams—cannot support a verdict. This post unpacks the evidentiary shortfalls and offers trial-practice takeaways for proving element-by-element mappings in DSP-heavy cases.

blogs.title: Three Signals, Not Three Uniques: Federal Circuit Rebuffs Disavowal in ’775 Claim
blogs.description: On claim construction, the court declined to read “three signals S1, S2 and S3” as requiring three unique inputs. Despite amendments adding “three signals” during prosecution, the panel found no clear and unambiguous disclaimer of two-signal implementations with a copied or derived third signal, aligning with Continental Circuits’ disavowal doctrine. The district court’s “separately identifiable, not necessarily unique” construction stands. We analyze the intrinsic and extrinsic bases for that outcome, its implications for drafting algorithmic claims (where copies, filtered versions, or conjugated streams abound), and the practical line between “separately identifiable” and “the same signal in disguise.”

blogs.title: Seven Means Seven: Why Conjugates and Moduli Didn’t Prove Infringement Under the ’775 Patent
blogs.description: The ’775 verdict fell because Finesse never proved the seven enumerated third-order products were performed. The Nokia materials showed three distinct operations—x1·|x1|·|x1|, x1·x1·x2′, and x1·|x2|·|x2|—involving modulus and complex conjugation, not the seven listed multiplications. No evidence showed repeated multiplications to reach all seven, and Finesse’s appellate mapping (including references to a ten-term polynomial) was never put to the jury and did not reconcile conjugates/moduli with the claim’s straight multiplications. This post explains the doctrinal lesson: in algorithm claims enumerating specific products, every operation must be proven with a clean, admissible mapping—especially when complex-valued DSP operations are involved.

blogs.title: JMOL, Substantial Evidence, and a $166M Reversal: Lessons from Finesse v. AT&T
blogs.description: Applying Fifth Circuit law, the Federal Circuit reviewed the denial of JMOL de novo and then asked whether substantial evidence supported the infringement findings. It answered no on both patents and vacated a $166.3 million lump-sum award. We situate the ruling within a broader trend of close scrutiny of expert mappings in E.D. Tex. mega-verdicts, discuss the preservation skirmish over the “uniqueness” theory, and highlight practice pointers: lock down clear element-by-element proofs at Rule 50(a), avoid overreliance on block-diagram legends, and ensure the jury actually receives any technical mapping you plan to defend on appeal.
